title: Reduce N to Zero by Subtracting Digits
statement:
You are given a positive integer `n`. In one operation you may choose any **non-zero digit** that appears in the current decimal representation of the number and subtract that digit from the number. (Subtracting `0` would change nothing, so it is never useful.) The number is re-read after every operation, so the digits available to you change as the number changes.

Find the **minimum number of operations** needed to reduce `n` to exactly `0`.

For example, `27` has digits `2` and `7`. Subtracting `7` gives `20`, whose only non-zero digit is `2`, and so on.
inputFormat: A single line containing the integer `n`.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the minimum number of operations.

examples.explanation: 27 → 20 (subtract 7) → 18 (subtract 2) → 10 (subtract 8) → 9 (subtract 1) → 0 (subtract 9). Five operations, and no sequence of four reaches 0.
The only non-zero digit of 10 is 1, giving 9. Then 9 − 9 = 0.
The digit 9 is available immediately, so one operation suffices.

hints: Let f(x) be the minimum number of operations to bring x down to 0. After one operation x becomes x − d for some non-zero digit d of x.
Many different paths pass through the same intermediate numbers, so computing f for every value from 1 up to n (bottom-up, or BFS from n with a visited set) avoids repeating work.
f(x) = 1 + min f(x − d) over the non-zero digits d of x. Each number has at most about log10(n) digits, so the table costs O(n log n).
